L9@P0: Abstract
L10@P0: This article analyzes and demonstrates the declining social selectivity of migration distance
L11@P0: in Europe’s long nineteenth century and argues that this drove a radically new process of
L12@P0: democratization of long-distance migration. It uses innovative spatial and quantitative
L13@P0: analysis of nominal data on more than 5,000 international migrants who moved to the
L14@P0: booming port city of Antwerp in present-day Belgium between 1850 and 1910. Examining
L15@P0: the changes in migrants’ origins and trajectories on the one hand, and in their profiles in
L16@P0: terms of gender and occupations on the other hand, it argues that the main evolutions
L17@P0: observed represent an overall loosening of the ancien régime link between migration
L18@P0: distance on the one hand and social selectivity on the other hand. By focusing on gender
L19@P0: and social class as markers of social selectivity and by mapping the impressive expansion
L20@P0: of the trajectories of Antwerp’s growing number of long-distance migrants, it lays bare
L21@P0: the spatial, gender, and social dimensions that contributed to a general process of
L22@P0: democratization of long-distance migration. As such, it sheds new light on the dynamics of
L23@P0: Europe’s so-called “mobility transition” in the long nineteenth century.
L24@P0: Keywords: urban history; migration history; mobility transition; long nineteenth century
L25@P0: Introduction
L26@P0: Europe’s long nineteenth century was characterized by an impressive rise in overall
L27@P0: migration (Lucassen and Lucassen 2009). Processes of demographic growth,
L28@P0: proletarianization, mechanization, and the disintegration of rural livelihoods, fueled
L29@P0: migration to cities and stimulated urban growth (Lees and Lees 2007). At the same
L30@P0: time, the marked expansion and improvement of means of communication and
L31@P0: transport facilitated migration and mobility, allowing more people to move over
L32@P0: longer distances (O’Rourke and Williamson 2001). While the scale and direction of
L33@P0: aggregate change during this so-called “mobility transition” (Zelinsky 1971) have

L42@P1: flows from a social and spatial perspective. In this article, we investigate the social
L43@P1: characteristics and spatial trajectories of international migrants to one booming
L44@P1: European port city during the second half of the “long nineteenth century” to
L45@P1: identify patterns of change in urban migration flows over time. We use this case
L46@P1: study to argue and illustrate how the loosening connection between migration
L47@P1: distance, social class, and gender, a process we call the democratization of
L48@P1: long-distance migration, was one of the most momentous changes characterizing the
L49@P1: unprecedented expansion of migration during the “mobility transition” of the long
L50@P1: nineteenth century.
L51@P1: Migration selectivity and the mobility transition
L52@P1: Historical patterns of migration differed considerably according to age, gender,
L53@P1: social position, and geographical background: migration is a selective, social process,
L54@P1: which channeled particular groups to specific destinations (Moch 2003). To account
L55@P1: for this selectivity, Hoerder (1997) has drawn attention to the so-called micro-level
L56@P1: and meso-level, next to structural macro-factors, to explain migration behavior.
L57@P1: Macro-factors refer to societal characteristics that govern the spatial distribution of
L58@P1: opportunities and constraints, such as employment, prices, and wages in economic
L59@P1: terms, or persecution in political terms, while the micro-level refers to individual
L60@P1: characteristics of migrants such as age, gender, skill, and wealth. In between stands
L61@P1: the meso-level, i.e., the social networks and information channels at the disposal of
L62@P1: (potential) migrants, which guide them in their migration decisions (Rosental 2006).
L63@P1: A special case is that of chain migration, when relatives or co-villagers already
L64@P1: resident elsewhere provide information and support to (future) migrants (Wegge
L65@P1: 1998). Yet, migration also regularly took place without personal or family
L66@P1: connections, guided by other channels of information, such as printed media,
L67@P1: professional networks, recruitment agencies, travelers’ tales, or even gossip (Lesger
L68@P1: 2006; Lesger et al. 2002). Crucially, access to such personal and impersonal networks
L69@P1: and information is socially selective, which helps to explain why and how different
L70@P1: migrant groups adapted their behavior to changing circumstances in different ways
L71@P1: and at different speeds (Winter 2009).
L72@P1: Distance has long been a distinctive feature in migration selectivity. Like other
L73@P1: spatial interactions, migration tends to be characterized by a distance-decay effect:
L74@P1: other things being equal, the likelihood of migration between any two places
L75@P1: declines as their distance increases (Fellman et al. 2003: 68–69). Yet, migration’s
L76@P1: sensitivity to distance and “intervening obstacles” is socially selective, which can be
L77@P1: related to differences in the relative costs and benefits of travel (Lee 1966) and
L78@P1: differential access to social networks and channels of information (Winter 2009).
L79@P1: Ravenstein’s(1885: 196–99) so-called “laws of migration” observed as early as the
L80@P1: late nineteenth century that women were as mobile as men but tended to move over
L81@P1: shorter distances, while men dominated long-distance migration between cities
L82@P1: (see also Alexander and Steidl 2012). Likewise, Winter (2013) has likened urban
L83@P1: immigration in early modern Europe to a social pyramid. Its broad base, genderbalanced or even female-predominant, consisted of short-distance, low-skilled,
L84@P1: 384 Hilde Greefs and Anne Winter
L85@P1-2: https://doi.org/10.1017/ssh.2024.9 Published online by Cambridge University Presslow-literate, and unspecialized rural migrants, whose continued influx was
L86@P2: necessary to oil the brawn-intensive preindustrial urban economy (Clark 1987;
L87@P2: De Vries 1984: 199–210; Poussou 1988). The top of this migration pyramid – its size
L88@P2: determined by the city’s demand for skill – consisted of long-distance,
L89@P2: predominantly male migrants who were better skilled, literate, and specialized,
L90@P2: and mostly moved in interurban patterns of career migration (Groot and Schalk
L91@P2: 2022: 211–14; Lesger 2006:8–11, 19–20; Lucassen and De Vries 2001; Luu 2004).
L92@P2: While the former depended primarily on diffuse channels of interpersonal, oral
L93@P2: communication, which were most dense between a city and its direct hinterland, the
L94@P2: latter had access to specialized, professional networks and information channels that
L95@P2: covered longer distances (Kooij 1996: 200–201; Winter 2009). More generally, the
L96@P2: bulk of rural migration in early modern Europe took place over short distances,
L97@P2: hence is dubbed “micro-mobility” rather than migration (Deschacht and Winter
L98@P2: 2019; Poussou 1988), while migration over longer distances was predominantly
L99@P2: interurban in character (Tilly 1978).
L100@P2: The positive correlation between migration distance, urban background, and
L101@P2: social status observed in early modern history, contrasts sharply with the image of
L102@P2: low-skilled and ragged rural masses crossing long distances and even oceans in
L103@P2: extensive numbers on the eve of World War I (Hoerder and Kaur 2013; McKeown
L104@P2: 2004; Steidl 2021), when women too became more prominent in long-distance
L105@P2: migrations within and from Europe (Donato and Gabaccia 2015; Gabaccia and
L106@P2: Zanoni 2012; Schrover 2013). In that respect, the long nineteenth century appears as
L107@P2: a transition period during which the longstanding connection between migration
L108@P2: distance and social status broke down, widening the migration horizons of millions
L109@P2: of Europeans from modest backgrounds, a process that we propose to label the
L110@P2: “democratization of long-distance migration.” In their quantitative study of
L111@P2: European migration levels over the past five centuries, Lucassen and Lucassen
L112@P2: (2009) conclusively debunked the myth of migration as a “modern” phenomenon of
L113@P2: the nineteenth century and demonstrated long-standing involvement with
L114@P2: migration since at least the sixteenth century. In this context, the real novelty of
L115@P2: the “mobility transition” of the long nineteenth century was possibly not so much
L116@P2: the observed increase in levels of mobility per se, as a restructuring and widening
L117@P2: of existing patterns of mobility, transforming earlier processes of (short-distance)
L118@P2: “micro-mobility” into (longer-distance) “migration” (cf. Deschacht and Winter
L119@P2: 2019).
L120@P2: At the macro-level, Europe’s Age of Mass Migration (Hatton and Williamson
L121@P2: 1998) was fueled by a fundamental restructuring of constraints – the increasing
L122@P2: precarity of rural livelihoods – and opportunities – the proliferation of industrial
L123@P2: and service jobs in cities home and abroad. Yet, the key to the emancipation from
L124@P2: the impediment of distance that underlay the mass nature of migration were the
L125@P2: many improvements in transport and communication technologies. These
L126@P2: fundamentally altered the dynamics at the meso-level and allowed rural migrants
L127@P2: to access information and support networks that transcended the regional
L128@P2: hinterland of the nearest towns (De Block and Polasky 2011; Schepers et al.
L129@P2: 2020). Newer, faster, and more reliable overland and waterway connections via
L130@P2: paved roads, railways, and steamships, and the strong competition between
L131@P2: transport and travel agencies, fostered a noticeable decrease in travel cost

L133@P2-3: https://doi.org/10.1017/ssh.2024.9 Published online by Cambridge University Press(Feys 2013; Martí-Henneberg 2021;O’Rourke and Williamson 2001: 35–36; Pooley
L134@P3: 2017). At the same time, growing literacy rates, the proliferation and improved
L135@P3: distribution of newspapers, postal services, telecommunications, and activities of
L136@P3: recruitment agencies facilitated and democratized access to information (Crafts
L137@P3: 1997: 305–7; Kaukiainen 2001:8–21; Wadauer et al. 2012: 168–71; Wenzlhuemer
L138@P3: 2007). As these changes facilitated the movement of goods, information, and people,
L139@P3: they significantly lowered the burden of distance and barriers to migration.
L140@P3: While long-distance migration in the nineteenth century has received attention
L141@P3: primarily in the context of transatlantic migration (e.g., Harzig 1997), in this study
L142@P3: we focus on analyzing the role of distance from a more inclusive, long-term
L143@P3: perspective, allowing us to evaluate shifts over time in migration range. Several
L144@P3: scholars have studied migration by specific groups, or to specific cities and regions
L145@P3: during the age of mass migration (e.g., Green 1998; Hochstadt 1999; Jackson 1997;
L146@P3: Pooley and Turnbull 1998; Steidl 2003, 2021), expanding our insight into the varied
L147@P3: experiences of Europe’s mass migrants. While they enrich our understanding in
L148@P3: many respects, no existing study explicitly tackles what we believe to be a central
L149@P3: feature of Europe’s mobility transition, namely the declining social selectivity of
L150@P3: distance. In this article, we combine a conventional analysis of urban migration
L151@P3: streams in the second half of the long nineteenth century with a novel focus on the
L152@P3: changing relationship between migration distance, social status, and gender. By
L153@P3: analyzing individual data on c. 5,000 international migrants moving to the booming
L154@P3: port city of Antwerp between 1850 and 1910, we aim to gain a better, differentiated
L155@P3: understanding of the social and gender dimensions that contributed to the
L156@P3: democratization of long-distance migration in the long nineteenth century.
L157@P3: Case study and sources
L158@P3: The city of Antwerp represents an interesting case for this study. During the second
L159@P3: half of the long nineteenth century, the former regional textile town developed into a
L160@P3: flourishing Atlantic port and trading center (Veraghtert 1986). The city became a
L161@P3: prime node in the Atlantic economy not only for the transshipment of goods but
L162@P3: also for that of passengers with the establishment of the Red Star Line (1873), which
L163@P3: would transport many hundreds of thousands of Europeans to America (Feys 2013).
L164@P3: New employment opportunities in the port economy, service sector, and portrelated industries heightened its appeal to newcomers, as did processes of economic
L165@P3: depression and proletarianization in its hinterland (Lis 1986). Its population
L166@P3: expanded rapidly from c. 100,000 mid-century to more than 300,000 on the eve of
L167@P3: World War I, which officially made it the largest city of the Kingdom of Belgium.
L168@P3: While Antwerp recorded some 5,000 newcomers per year in the 1850s – both
L169@P3: national and international – this increased to more than 8,000 in the 1870s and
L170@P3: 1880s and more than 20,000 in the first decade of the twentieth century. An
L171@P3: important share of this growing number of newcomers came from abroad. Because
L172@P3: of Belgium’s relatively small size and Antwerp’s location near the border, foreign
L173@P3: newcomers extended from quasi-neighbors who had traveled less than 50 km, to
L174@P3: those who had crossed continents and oceans. Annual published figures, available
L175@P3: from 1864 onwards, show a steady increase in international migration over the

L177@P3-4: https://doi.org/10.1017/ssh.2024.9 Published online by Cambridge University Pressperiod (Graph 1). Recorded immigration from abroad fluctuated around 1,000 in
L178@P4: the early 1860s, increasing to around 3,000 to 4,000 in the 1890s, and surpassing
L179@P4: 6,000 in the years leading up to World War I. Over the same period, the proportion
L180@P4: of foreign nationals in the city’s overall population expanded from 6.82% in the
L181@P4: 1856 census to 11.16% in 1910 (Greefs and Winter 2020a; Statistique de la Belgique
L182@P4: 1856–1910; Verslag over het bestuur en den zakentoestand der Stad Antwerpen
L183@P4: 1865–1911).
L184@P4: In the first half of the nineteenth century, international migration to Antwerp
L185@P4: was dominated by male migrants who worked as merchants, clerks, and hospitality
L186@P4: workers in the city’s expanding commercial firms, insurance companies, banks,
L187@P4: shipbuilding companies, and bourgeois cafés and restaurants – i.e., a classic pattern
L188@P4: of social selectivity in long-distance migration (Winter 2009). A similar “elite”
L189@P4: nature of foreign migration was also noticed in the capital city of Brussels in the
L190@P4: same period (De Schaepdrijver 1990). After observing that single foreign migration
L191@P4: to Antwerp feminized considerably between 1850 and 1880 (Greefs and Winter
L192@P4: 2016), we embarked on the current, more encompassing research endeavor in which
L193@P4: we extend our time frame to 1910 and include all international newcomers, in order
L194@P4: to make the evolution of the social selectivity of distance over time our prime focus.
L195@P4: The empirical basis of this study derives from Antwerp’s foreigners’ files (dossiers
L196@P4: des étrangers), kept in the city archives from the 1840s onwards. For each foreigner
L197@P4: who came to reside within a municipality of the Belgian state, a personal
L198@P4: information form (bulletin de renseignements) had to be filled out by the local police,
L199@P4: and forwarded to the national agency monitoring immigration, the Sûreté Publique
L200@P4: (Caestecker 2000). The bulletin contained answers to pre-printed questions on the
L201@P4: identity (name, age, and sex), social and family background (parents, marital status,
L202@P4: and occupation), and migration trajectories (place of birth and of last residence
L203@P4: abroad and in Belgium) of the foreigner and his/her family, next to more lapidary
L204@P4: information on judicial antecedents, reputation, or documentary status. Whereas

L209@P5: the years up to 1890 (Willems et al. 2018), the local series of foreigners’ files have
L210@P5: been conserved in their entirety in Antwerp.
L211@P5: The foreigners’ files were but one component of the precocious and laborious
L212@P5: administrative infrastructure of population registration in nineteenth-century
L213@P5: Belgium, which also included the civil registry of births, marriages, and deaths,
L214@P5: 10-yearly population censuses, dynamic population registers, passport provisions
L215@P5: and visa registration, and municipal demographic statistics including yearly
L216@P5: immigration and emigration (Bracke 2008; Debackere 2020; Eggerickx and
L217@P5: Sanderson 2010). Destined specifically for the registration of foreign residents
L218@P5: who intended to stay for a while – the normative cut-off was longer than a fortnight
L219@P5: – the foreigners’ files inherently exclude highly mobile and transitory groups, such
L220@P5: as short-stay visitors, sailors, wanderers, or passengers waiting for departure.1 Those
L221@P5: who did fall within the scope of the foreigners’ files, mostly presented themselves for
L222@P5: registration soon after arrival and on their own initiative, possibly prompted by
L223@P5: landlords, acquaintances, employers, local constables, travel guides, and/or an
L224@P5: internalized expectation of registration. The information noted down in the bulletin
L225@P5: was verified on the basis of identity documents produced by the migrant, and/or
L226@P5: inquiries with (previous) employers, landlords, or local authorities of previous
L227@P5: places of residence. When foreigners arrived as a family unit, a bulletin was
L228@P5: compiled only for the head of household, with mention of spouse and/or children.
L229@P5: As far as we could gauge, registration did not entail any obvious disadvantages,
L230@P5: except for those liable to be considered as vagrants or criminals. Although some
L231@P5: intentionally or unintentionally evaded registration, the sheer volume of the
L232@P5: bulletins des étrangers together with the city’s well-developed population
L233@P5: administration, warrant that they were a small minority at most.2 It is therefore
L234@P5: safe to assume that the bulletins des étrangers recorded the lion’s share of all foreign
L235@P5: migrants and can be taken as indicative of the evolution of foreign migration to
L236@P5: Antwerp in this period.
L237@P5: We collected, cleaned, and analyzed all nominal data from the foreigners’ files for
L238@P5: three sample years, 1850, 1880, and 1910, chosen to represent years not
L239@P5: characterized by specific crisis contexts and at equal intervals to explore changes
L240@P5: over time (henceforth DFFA, Database Foreigners’ Files Antwerp, 1850–1910).3
L241@P5: This resulted in a total sample of 5,883 records: 680 for 1850, 1,723 for 1880, and

L258@P6: This database provides the empirical basis for the discussion below. We will first
L259@P6: discuss the main evolutions in migrants’ origins, before relating these to their
L260@P6: profiles in terms of gender and occupation between 1850 and 1910. Next to the
L261@P6: impressive expansion and broadening of Antwerp’s migration field, we will argue
L262@P6: that the main evolutions observed here represent an overall loosening of the ancien
L263@P6: régime link between migration distance on the one hand, and social selectivity on
L264@P6: the other hand. This resulted in an overall democratization of long-distance
L265@P6: migration, in the sense that more people with lesser means tended to move over
L266@P6: larger distances. By focusing on gender and social class as markers of social
L267@P6: selectivity and by examining the stepwise nature of the moves of these growing
L268@P6: numbers of long-distance migrants, we gain more insights into the new trajectories
L269@P6: of these “modest” migrant groups.
L270@P6: Nets cast wider: an expanding and broadening migration field
L271@P6: While the overall number of foreign newcomers to Antwerp grew considerably
L272@P6: between 1850 and 1910, so did the area where they hailed from. Comparing
L273@P6: Maps 1.1–1.3 illustrates an impressive expansion of the city’s migration field, in
L274@P6: which there was a decreasing relative importance of nearby border regions and an
L275@P6: increasing importance of more distant regions of origin, especially from the northeast.5 With Antwerp located only 20 km south of the Dutch border, “international”
L276@P6: migration from the Dutch border regions had been part of Antwerp’s regional
L277@P6: migration field for centuries. We know for instance from earlier research that these
L278@P6: regions supplied more than two-thirds (68%) of foreign residents in the 1796
L279@P6: census, when Antwerp was merely a regional textile center (Winter 2009). Whereas
L280@P6: Dutch border regions in 1850 still supplied 41% of all foreign newcomers, by 1880
L281@P6: this was only 28%, and in 1910 barely 12%.6 In 1880 they were complemented
L282@P6: mainly by growing numbers from the German border regions (24%),7 with which
L283@P6: intense commercial interaction was invigorated by Antwerp’s revived port activity
L284@P6: and an early railway connection (the “Iron Rhine,” in 1843) (Devos and Greefs 2000;
L285@P6: Vrints 2002). By 1910, Antwerp’s migration field clearly surpassed not only the
L286@P6: cross-border regions but also the neighboring countries. Most conspicuously, by
